description: Hi! I'm Afshan, a solo participant from Multan, Pakistan, building "Listen to the Earth", my take on the Earth Information Jukebox. Click anywhere on a map and hear NASA Earth data as music: temperature, sea ice and rainfall become different instruments, and a time slider lets you hear how our planet has changed. I'm using JavaScript, Web Audio and data visualization to make Earth science accessible to everyone.
summary: Listen to the Earth is my Earth Information Jukebox: an interactive world map that turns NASA Earth data into music. Tap any place and hear its climate. Temperature becomes a warm pad, rainfall becomes bells, wind becomes breath, and sea ice, ocean heat and plants add glass chimes, a deep drone and wooden plucks. A time slider (1981 to 2024) lets you hear how a place has changed, and the Climate Duet plays a past year in one ear and today in the other, so warming can be heard. The page shows the country and the weather, reads places aloud, works with arrow keys and can vibrate on phones. It makes Earth science accessible to blind and low-vision users and to everyone. Most importantly It is made to help blind and low-vision people, students and everyone understand a changing planet."
details:
What it does: You tap anywhere on a world map and hear the climate of that place as music, while the page shows the country name and the monthly weather in words. Six instruments play at once: temperature is a warm pad (warmer is higher), rainfall is bells, wind is airy breath, sea ice is glass chimes, ocean heat is a deep drone and plants are wooden plucks. A year slider (1981 to 2024) and a month slider let you hear change over time. An Earth story tour plays a guided trip (Multan, the Amazon, the Southern Ocean, the Arctic ice, the 2022 floods in Sindh, and a final duet). The Climate Duet plays a past year in the left ear and a later year in the right ear, and the difference is the warming. You can also enter your birth year and hear it against today.

Accessibility: The page can read a place aloud, can be used with the arrow keys and Enter, and can vibrate on phones with rainfall, so the data is not only visual.

Data and tools: Built with JavaScript, the Web Audio API, HTML Canvas and the browser speech feature. Temperature, rainfall and wind for the tapped place come from NASA POWER monthly data. Sea ice, ocean heat and plant cover are estimated by a simple model from that data and are not direct NASA measurements. The map colours are a model preview. Country outlines are from Natural Earth.

Natural Earth country outlines

Who made it: Concept, design decisions and testing by Afshan, a solo participant from Multan, Pakistan. The code was written with AI assistance (Claude, by Anthropic). All sounds are generated in the browser by code, with no copyrighted audio.
Benefits and intended impact: The project makes climate data available through sound, so blind and low-vision people, students and anyone who finds graphs hard can understand how a place has changed. Hearing 1981 and today at the same time (the Climate Duet) makes warming something people can feel, which can help teachers and communities talk about climate change. It is a teaching and awareness tool, not a research tool. It is an early prototype and has not yet been tested with blind or low-vision users, so the next step is to collect their feedback and replace the modelled parts (sea ice, ocean heat, plants) with real NASA data.
